nodes.title: Exploitation techniques: Key Ideas
nodes.content: The exploitation phase of a pentest is where reconnaissance becomes access. You're chaining a vulnerability with a payload to land code execution. The exam tests common categories (buffer overflows, injection, deserialization, privilege escalation) and the tools that automate them.

flashcards.front: Buffer overflow — what's the basic mechanism?
flashcards.back: An unbounded write past the end of a stack buffer overwrites the saved return address. When the function returns, execution jumps to whatever the attacker placed there — typically shellcode or a return-into-libc gadget. Modern mitigations: stack canaries, ASLR, DEP/NX — defeated one at a time by chaining bugs.

flashcards.front: SQL injection vs command injection — same idea?
flashcards.back: Same root cause: untrusted input concatenated into a command string the interpreter executes. SQLi puts `OR 1=1` into a query. Command injection puts `; cat /etc/passwd` into a shell call. Mitigations also the same shape: parameterized queries, never build commands by string concatenation.

Going from a low-priv shell to root / SYSTEM / admin. Two flavors: vertical (low → high on the same machine via a kernel bug, sudo misconfig, SUID binary) and horizontal (account A → account B at same privilege level). The 'pentester's daily bread' — initial access is usually a low-priv user.

flashcards.front: Why is Metasploit so commonly mentioned in exam questions?
flashcards.back: It's the dominant exploit framework — modular: pick an exploit module, set a payload (Meterpreter, reverse shell), set options (RHOSTS, LHOST), run. It bundles thousands of vetted exploits and post-modules. The exam tests vocabulary (msfconsole, payload, listener, handler) more than deep usage.

nodes.title: Cryptography fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Crypto is the math layer that makes the rest of security possible. Most exam questions test symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing vs encryption, when to use which, and how key management actually works in practice.

flashcards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Symmetric (AES-256, ChaCha20): one shared key, fast, used for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): public/private key pair, slow, used to exchange a symmetric key or to sign. Real systems use both: asymmetric to negotiate, symmetric to encrypt the bulk traffic (this is how TLS works).

flashcards.front: What's the difference between hashing and encryption?
flashcards.back: Encryption is reversible — the holder of the key can recover the plaintext. Hashing is one-way — you cannot derive the input from the output. Hashes are for integrity (did the file change?) and password storage (compare hashes, never store plaintext). SHA-256 is the modern default; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken.

A signature is a hash of the message encrypted with the signer's private key. Anyone with the public key can verify (decrypt the signature, recompute the hash, check they match). This proves authenticity (the holder of the private key signed it) AND integrity (the message wasn't tampered with).

flashcards.front: Why use a key management service (KMS)?
flashcards.back: Raw key handling is hard to do safely — you have to rotate, audit, restrict, destroy. A KMS holds keys in hardware, exposes encrypt/decrypt APIs, logs every use, enforces who can use which key. Your application code never sees the actual key material. AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS all play this role.

nodes.title: VPN and secure connectivity: Key Ideas
nodes.content: A VPN tunnels private traffic over the public internet, encrypting it end-to-end. Site-to-site VPNs connect networks (e.g., on-prem to cloud); client VPNs connect individual devices to a private network. Both rely on IPsec or SSL/TLS.

flashcards.front: Site-to-site VPN vs client VPN — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: Site-to-site VPN connects two networks (typical: on-prem data center ↔ cloud VPC) using gateway devices on each side. Client VPN connects an individual user's laptop to a private network for remote access. Site-to-site uses IPsec, client VPN often uses SSL or WireGuard.

Phase 1 (IKE) authenticates the two peers (pre-shared key or certificate) and builds a secure management channel. Phase 2 negotiates the actual data tunnel (encryption algorithm, key lifetime). Most exam questions test that phase 1 must succeed before phase 2.

flashcards.front: When do you pick a dedicated link over a VPN?
flashcards.back: VPN over the public internet is cheap but variable — bandwidth and latency depend on internet weather. Dedicated links (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute, Cloud Interconnect) are private fiber with consistent latency and bandwidth — pick them for production traffic that must be predictable, or compliance scenarios that forbid the public internet.

flashcards.front: What's the BGP tunnel option for?
flashcards.back: VPNs can use static routes or BGP. BGP-based VPNs auto-propagate route changes between sides (add a new subnet on-prem → cloud learns it within seconds). Static VPN requires manual route updates every time the topology changes. Always pick BGP for production.

nodes.title: Identity providers and federation: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Modern identity is centralized — one identity provider issues tokens that every application trusts. SAML and OIDC are the two interop standards. Federation means trusting another organization's identity provider for cross-org access.

flashcards.front: SAML vs OIDC — what's the practical difference?
flashcards.back: SAML: XML, browser-redirect-heavy, used for enterprise SSO into web apps. OIDC (on top of OAuth 2.0): JSON, mobile- and SPA-friendly, the modern default. New integrations should use OIDC; existing SAML works fine, no urgent reason to migrate.

flashcards.front: What's an IdP vs an SP (service provider)?
flashcards.back: Identity Provider: where users actually authenticate (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, Auth0). Service Provider: the app the user is trying to use (Slack, Salesforce, your custom app). The IdP issues a signed token; the SP trusts the IdP's signature and reads the user's identity from the token.

flashcards.front: MFA — why is push notification preferred over SMS?
flashcards.back: SMS is sniffable (SS7 attacks) and SIM-swappable. Push (Duo, Microsoft Authenticator, OS-level biometric) is bound to a specific device, requires user interaction, harder to phish. WebAuthn / FIDO2 hardware keys are the gold standard — phishing-resistant by design.

flashcards.front: Just-in-time (JIT) provisioning — what does it solve?
flashcards.back: Instead of pre-creating users in every app, JIT creates the user on first SSO login, hydrated from the IdP's attributes. Onboarding a new hire: add to the IdP group once, every app that supports JIT auto-creates them on first visit. Deprovisioning is the inverse — IdP removes them, apps refuse next login.
